newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's tax plan trims business tax breaks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's tax plan trims business tax breaks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is ready to send Congress a proposal to close $39 billion worth of tax breaks for businesses over five years to help pay for nearly $100 billion in broader tax cuts, Democratic congressional sources said on Friday.
Administration officials told congressional staff in detailed briefings this week that the changes were very similar to those proposed by the president last year, which were not enacted by Congress.
Closing these tax loopholes will be part of an expected $80 billion in tax increases that administration sources said will also renew the airline ticket tax and other excise taxes.

Clinton is to send his fiscal 1998 budget to Congress next Thursday and has pledged that it will show the way to balance the budget by the year 2002. To do this, and provide nearly $100 billion in tax relief over five years, his plan must find revenue or make deeper cuts in spending.

One of the most controversial proposals would require investors, particularly those holding mutual funds, to use the average price of a stock when figuring gains or losses upon sale, called "average cost basis." Now, investors have more flexibility in calculating for tax purposes the sale price of their stocks.

As in last year's White House budget, the plan will also restrict the interest deductions companies get from investments in tax-exempt bonds. In addition, congressional staff said Treasury officials informed them Clinton would seek to repeal the subsidy multinational companies receive for exports to foreign units.

Another profitable tax break for investors, called "selling short against the box," would be eliminated in Clinton's plan. Rather than selling stock that is owned, investors are able to sell identical stock they have borrowed with their own stock used as collateral.
The briefings for Democratic congressional staff, and subsequent leak to reporters, upset a key Republican whose own staff had not been informed of the tax details.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, found it an "unwelcome" sign that details of the administration's tax proposal were not given to Republicans in Congress, a senior House Republican aide said.
"Republicans were not informed of any of the information," the aide said.

Archer has said he favours closing tax loopholes, but does not intend to raise taxes on "job-makers, risk takers and investors" as a way to balance the budget. He also said last week he doubted a tax bill could be passed that did not give broader capital gains tax relief than Clinton will propose.
Expired excise taxes will likely be considered later in the year during budget negotiations, another Republican aide said.

Clinton will also seek tax relief for many families through a $500 per child tax credit, a $1,500 tax credit for college tuition and raising the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $250,000 per person, or $500,000 per couple, for all Americans.

At present, persons under 55 can roll over gains into a higher priced home and those over 55 can exclude $125,000 of profits upon sale. A maximum $5,000 tax credit for companies hiring peoeple on welfare will also be offered.
Senate Republicans have proposed their own $173 billion tax relief package over five years with a child tax credit and capital gains tax rate reductions.
